fixes.explanation: Jacob, the father of these brothers, says it plainly: “Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.” (Genesis 42:2) Life is on the line, and the errand is just as clear. One job, friend, and it's buying grain. No side quests.

Jacob says nothing about selling flocks. His words are about going down to Egypt and buying grain, so that they “…may live and not die.” (Genesis 42:2) Trading flocks for silver is a whole different business plan, and Jacob never pitches it. The plan on the table is one trip and one purchase.

Verse 3 says it straight: “So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.” Ten brothers is a lot of people for one shopping list. Benjamin isn't in that number, as the next verse shows (Genesis 42:4).

Seven is a lucky number, baker, but it's not the one in the text. Verse 3 says, “So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.” Seven would leave the group three men short. Ten is the number, and ten is a LOT of brothers on one road.

That's right. Verse 6 says that when the brothers arrived, “…they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.” Joseph was the ruler of the land, the one selling the grain. Ten men bowing low in front of him, and verse 8 says they did not recognize him (Genesis 42:8).

They don't ask for Pharaoh, Egypt's king. Joseph is the ruler of the land and the one selling grain, so the man they need is already standing in front of them (Genesis 42:6). What they do is bow down “…with their faces to the ground.” Nobody needs to go over his head when he's right there.

No gifts show up in this scene. The text says they “…bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.” (Genesis 42:6) They came to buy grain, and bowing is the first thing the verse shows them doing.

The text says Joseph “…spoke harshly to them.” (Genesis 42:7) His first words are a question: “Where have you come from?” That's not a friendly greeting at the front desk. It's a hard question from the man in charge.
Guests would get a warm welcome, and that's not what verse 7 describes. Joseph “…treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them.” (Genesis 42:7) Not exactly a welcome basket, friend.

Joseph swears, “As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.” (Genesis 42:15) Pharaoh is Egypt's king, and Joseph uses his life as the oath. This is how he says the brothers will be tested. The test starts with one name: the youngest.

Two is a good guess, baker, but Joseph's number is smaller. He says, “…leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households.” (Genesis 42:19) Just one stays, and the rest head home with grain.

They say it themselves: “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.” (Genesis 42:21) Their trouble in Egypt gets tied right back to how they treated him. They remember his pleading and say they would not listen.

Verse 22 says Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen…” (Genesis 42:22) Reuben is one of the brothers standing there. He's the one reminding everybody that he spoke up.
These words aren't Judah's. Verse 22 says Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy?…” (Genesis 42:22) The text gives them to Reuben, so he's your answer.
The text gives these words to someone else. Verse 22 says Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy?…” (Genesis 42:22) Levi isn't the one named as speaking here. Reuben is.

That's right. Verse 23 says, “They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them.” So they have no idea he understands. I think that's a very quiet kind of hard.

The statement is true, so False doesn't fit. Verse 23 says, “They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them.” (Genesis 42:23) The brothers have no idea he understands.
Verse 24 says Joseph “…took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.” Simeon is the brother who stays. The others have to watch it happen, and I think that's a hard thing to watch.

Verse 25 says Joseph gave orders “…to return each man’s silver to his sack…” So the bags get filled with grain, and the silver goes right back in the sacks. I bet somebody's in for a surprise when a sack gets opened.

No robes are mentioned in Joseph's order. Verse 25 says he gave orders “…to fill their bags with grain, to return each man’s silver to his sack, and to give them provisions for their journey.” The silver is what goes back in. The packing list says grain, silver and provisions, and that's it.

Nobody blames him. Verse 28 says their hearts sank, and trembling, they turned to one another. They said, “What is this that God has done to us?” (Genesis 42:28) They turn to each other, and they're shaken together. The question is about what has happened to all of them.

The brothers repeat the man's words to Jacob: “Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.” (Genesis 42:34) Their brother comes back, and they can trade there. It comes with a condition, which is bringing the youngest brother back to him.

A place to live near the ruler isn't in the offer. The brothers say the man told them, “Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.” (Genesis 42:34) The promise is their brother back and the right to trade.
That's right. Verse 35 says that when they and their father saw the bags of silver, “…they were dismayed.” Jacob and his sons all feel it. Nobody's throwing a party over that silver, baker.
That's not what Reuben says. His offer is, “You may kill my two sons…” (Genesis 42:37) It's heavy, and it puts his own family on the line. I think he's trying to show his father how serious he is.

Right, Jacob refuses. He says, “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left.” (Genesis 42:38) Reuben made his offer, and Jacob's answer is still no. The story isn't over, though.
